name: Linear Relationships
description: When one quantity changes at a constant rate with another (straight line)

content.overview: Ever notice how some things just change at a totally steady pace — like a taxi meter ticking up the same amount every minute? That's a linear relationship, and it's about as simple as physics gets: one quantity is just a constant multiple of another, plus maybe a starting amount. On a graph, it's always a straight line. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
**The equation you'll see everywhere:** y = mx + b

- m = slope (how steep the line is)
- b = y-intercept (where the line starts, on the y-axis)
- x = your input
- y = your output

**Where you'll spot this in physics:** {{viz:chart-01}}
- Distance = speed × time, at constant speed: d = st (a straight line through the origin)
- Celsius to Kelvin: K = C + 273.15 (straight line, just shifted up)
- Force = mass × acceleration: F = ma (straight line through the origin)
- Total cost = number of items × price per item (straight line, obviously)

**How do you know it's linear?** Easy checklist:
- The graph is a straight line, no curving
- Every time x goes up by 1, y goes up by the exact same amount
- The change is completely predictable, no surprises

**Why you'll be glad linear relationships exist:** {{viz:anim-01}}
- They're easy to picture in your head
- The math is dead simple
- They show up constantly in physics
- Once you know m and b, you know literally everything about the relationship — no guessing

So next time you spot "y = mx + b" in a problem, relax a little. That's a straight line, and straight lines are the friendliest thing physics throws at you.
keyPoints: Linear relationship: y = mx + b — that's the whole recipe
Graph is always a straight line, no exceptions
m is the slope — the rate of change
b is the y-intercept — the starting value
The rate of change never wobbles, it stays constant
You'll run into linear relationships constantly in physics
content.whyItMatters: A huge chunk of physics laws are linear, or close enough to it. The moment you recognize "oh, this is just y = mx + b," a problem that looked scary suddenly becomes a two-line solve.
